questions.enonce_markdown:
Determine the composition and describe the roles played by the following digestive secretions in the human body.

(i) Saliva.

(ii) Gastric juice.

(iii) Bile juice.

(iv) Pancreatic juice.

(v) Intestinal juice. *(4, 4, 4, 4, 4 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Saliva** (secreted by the parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands; pH about 6.5 to 7.5)

*Composition:* about **99% water**; **mucus (mucin)**; **salivary amylase**; **lysozyme**; mineral ions (Na+, K+, Cl-, HCO3-, phosphate) that make it a weak buffer; traces of urea and uric acid.

*Roles:*
- Water **dissolves food** so that it can be tasted, and **moistens and lubricates** it; mucus **binds the food into a bolus** that is easy to swallow.
- **Salivary amylase** (activated by Cl-) begins the hydrolysis of **starch to maltose**.
- **Lysozyme** digests bacterial cell walls and so has an **antibacterial** action; saliva also **cleans the mouth and teeth**.
- The hydrogencarbonate and phosphate ions keep the mouth at a near neutral pH, which suits amylase and protects the enamel of the teeth.

**(ii) Gastric juice** (secreted by the gastric glands of the stomach wall; pH about 1.5 to 2)

*Composition:* water; **hydrochloric acid** (from the oxyntic or parietal cells); **pepsinogen** (inactive, from the chief or peptic cells); **rennin** (chymosin, mainly in infants); a little **gastric lipase**; **mucus** (from the goblet cells); **intrinsic factor**.

*Roles:*
- **HCl** gives the acid pH needed by pepsin, **activates pepsinogen to pepsin**, **kills most bacteria** swallowed with food, and softens food and denatures proteins.
- **Pepsin** is an endopeptidase: it hydrolyses **proteins to shorter polypeptides**.
- **Rennin** **curdles milk** (caseinogen to casein, in the presence of Ca2+), so that milk stays longer in the stomach and is digested by pepsin.
- **Mucus** forms a protective layer that prevents the stomach wall from being digested by pepsin and damaged by acid.
- **Intrinsic factor** is needed for the absorption of **vitamin B12** in the ileum (needed for the formation of red blood cells).

**(iii) Bile juice** (made continuously by the liver, stored and concentrated in the gall bladder, released into the duodenum through the bile duct; pH about 7.6 to 8.6)

*Composition:* water; **bile salts** (sodium glycocholate and sodium taurocholate); **bile pigments** (bilirubin and biliverdin, from the breakdown of haemoglobin); **cholesterol**; **lecithin**; mucus; sodium hydrogencarbonate and other salts. **Bile contains no digestive enzymes.**

*Roles:*
- It **neutralises the acid chyme** from the stomach and gives the **alkaline medium** in which pancreatic and intestinal enzymes work best.
- **Bile salts emulsify fats**: they lower the surface tension of fat and break large globules into tiny droplets, which **increases the surface area** for **lipase**.
- Bile salts form **micelles** with fatty acids, monoglycerides and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), which helps their **absorption**.
- It is a route of **excretion** of bile pigments, cholesterol and some drugs; it also has a mild antiseptic effect.

**(iv) Pancreatic juice** (secreted by the exocrine cells of the pancreas into the duodenum through the pancreatic duct; pH about 8)

*Composition:* water; **sodium hydrogencarbonate**; the enzymes **pancreatic amylase**, **pancreatic lipase**, **trypsinogen** and **chymotrypsinogen** (inactive), **carboxypeptidase**, and **nucleases** (ribonuclease and deoxyribonuclease).

*Roles:*
- Hydrogencarbonate **neutralises the acid chyme** and gives the alkaline pH needed by the enzymes.
- **Amylase** hydrolyses starch to maltose; **lipase** hydrolyses fats (emulsified by bile) to fatty acids and glycerol (or monoglycerides).
- **Trypsinogen** is activated to **trypsin** by **enterokinase** (from the intestinal juice); trypsin then activates more trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen. **Trypsin and chymotrypsin** hydrolyse polypeptides to shorter peptides, and **carboxypeptidase** removes amino acids from the carboxyl end. Secretion as inactive precursors protects the pancreas from self digestion.
- **Nucleases** hydrolyse nucleic acids to nucleotides.

**(v) Intestinal juice (succus entericus)** (secreted by the glands of Brunner in the duodenum and by the crypts of Lieberkuhn in the ileum; pH about 8)

*Composition:* water; **mucus**; hydrogencarbonate and other salts; **enterokinase** (enteropeptidase); the peptidases **aminopeptidase and dipeptidase** (erepsin); the carbohydrases **maltase, sucrase and lactase**; a little **lipase**; **nucleotidases**. Many of these enzymes are held in the membrane of the epithelial cells (brush border) or released when the cells break down.

*Roles:*
- Mucus and hydrogencarbonate **protect the duodenal wall** from acid and **lubricate** the chyme.
- **Enterokinase** activates trypsinogen.
- **Peptidases** complete protein digestion: peptides to **amino acids**.
- **Maltase, sucrase and lactase** hydrolyse the disaccharides to the monosaccharides **glucose, fructose and galactose**; lipase finishes fat digestion; nucleotidases split nucleotides to sugar, phosphate and bases.
- Final digestion happens next to the absorbing surface, so the products are absorbed at once.

(Marking: about two marks for the composition and two for the roles of each secretion.)
